title: Polynomial-time derandomization of randomized \(\mathrm{AC}^0\)
formal: Does \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0\subseteq\mathrm P\) hold for polynomial-time-uniform circuit families? Equivalently, must every Boolean function on finite binary strings that is computed with error at most \(1/3\) on each input by a uniform polynomial-size, constant-depth randomized AND–OR circuit family admit an exact deterministic polynomial-time algorithm?
why: Constant-depth AND–OR circuits are a central restricted model for which strong lower bounds are known, yet fully eliminating their randomness in uniform polynomial time remains a distinct challenge. The question tests whether those structural restrictions suffice to remove random choices while allowing a much more flexible deterministic simulator.
status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The source explicitly poses the polynomial-time-uniform containment. The checked later generator and earlier weak-derandomization results have different quantitative or correctness guarantees. No proof or refutation of the stated containment was found in the bounded search; this does not certify exhaustive current openness.

progress.text: Shaltiel obtains explicit weak derandomization for constant-depth computations, preserving correctness on most inputs rather than every input.
The source records quasipolynomial simulation and explicitly asks whether polynomial-time uniform simulation is possible.
Lyu proves the \(O((\log S)^{d-1}\log(S/\varepsilon)\log\log S)\) seed bound for fooling fixed-depth circuits. The theorem does not give the polynomial-time class containment requested here.

sentences: The question asks whether randomness can be removed from uniform shallow AND–OR computations using deterministic polynomial time.
Each randomized circuit must answer correctly with probability at least two thirds on every input.
A single polynomial-time procedure constructs the family’s circuit descriptions from the input length.
The deterministic simulator may use arbitrary polynomial-time computation and need not remain a constant-depth circuit.
Quasipolynomial simulation, correctness on most inputs and nonuniform deterministic circuits do not meet the full target.

definitions: A Boolean function here is a total function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}\). A randomized circuit \(C_n(x,r)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output, \(n\) data input bits \(x\), and \(m(n)\) random input bits \(r\). Input nodes may contain these bits, their negations, and constants zero and one. Internal nodes are unbounded-fan-in AND or OR gates. There are no parity, majority, threshold or oracle gates. The depth is the maximum number of internal gates on an input-to-output path, and the size is the number of internal gates. Repeated wires into one gate are omitted. The entire circuit is encoded by an explicit ordered list of nodes, labels and predecessor lists with binary indices. A family witnesses \(f\in\mathrm{BPAC}^0\) if there exist fixed positive integers \(a,b,d\), a constant \(K\ge1\), and one deterministic algorithm \(M\) such that, for every \(n\ge0\), \(M\) given \(1^n\) outputs the circuit \(C_n\) in at most \(K(n+2)^a\) Turing-machine steps; its depth is at most \(d\), and both its size and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+2)^b\). On every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), independent fair random bits \(R\), uniform in \(\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\), satisfy \(\Pr[C_n(x,R)=f(x)]\ge2/3\). The constants, circuit-generation algorithm and random-bit bound may depend on the family but not on \(n\), \(x\) or the random choices. Polynomial-time uniformity is required; merely having a circuit at each length is insufficient. The class \(\mathrm P\) consists of the functions computed correctly on every binary input by one deterministic multitape Turing machine in at most \(K_0(n+2)^{b_0}\) worst-case steps, for some constants \(K_0,b_0\). That machine has no random bits, advice or oracle. It may depend on the randomized family, and its polynomial exponent need not be the same for all families. The target concerns class containment, with no additional demand for an algorithm that takes arbitrary family-generating programs and produces their deterministic simulators. The notation \(\mathrm{AC}^0\), used in the context below, means the analogous polynomial-time-uniform family with no random inputs.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0\subseteq\mathrm P\), or of its negation under the stated uniformity convention. A positive answer must give exact, all-input polynomial-time simulation for every such family. A negative answer requires a total function in uniform \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0\) with no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. Average-case correctness, quasipolynomial simulation, deterministic circuits without a uniform construction, or a failure to build one particular pseudorandom generator is insufficient. A proof of the stronger uniform equality \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0=\mathrm{AC}^0\) also answers the stated containment question, but preservation of constant depth is not required.

context_blocks.text: The randomized computation is shallow, but its random input can contain polynomially many bits. Trying every possible random string can therefore require far more than polynomial time. The desired simulator need only compute the same final bit; it is not required to retain the shallow circuit shape.

Uniformity is essential. A polynomial-time algorithm must be able to obtain the description for each length from that length alone. An existence theorem for a separately chosen circuit or separately chosen good random strings at every length does not provide such an algorithm.

Vadhan’s Definition 7.26 explicitly permits polynomial-time uniform construction. Open Problem 7.31 asks for the stronger equality \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0=\mathrm{AC}^0\), or at least containment in \(\mathrm P\). This card selects the latter, already stated alternative, matching its original polynomial-time title.

The source’s Corollary 7.30 gives a deterministic quasipolynomial-time simulation: time \(2^{(\log(n+2))^{O(1)}}\), with constants depending on the fixed family. It also records a quasipolynomial-size constant-depth simulation. Neither guarantee supplies polynomial time.

Shaltiel’s work gives uniform weak derandomization for constant-depth computations, where the deterministic result is correct on most inputs. It also notes that the nonuniform randomized and deterministic constant-depth classes coincide. Those statements leave this card’s simultaneous uniformity and all-input correctness requirement unresolved.

Lyu’s 2022 Theorem 1 constructs generators fooling depth-\(d\), size-\(S\) circuits within error \(\varepsilon\), with seed length \(O((\log S)^{d-1}\log(S/\varepsilon)\log\log S)\), for fixed \(d\) and \(S\) large enough. Here “fooling” means that every circuit’s acceptance probability changes by at most \(\varepsilon\). This is a substantial quantitative improvement, but its general fixed-depth seed bound is not \(O(\log S)\).

A pseudorandom generator is a useful comparison point, but its optimal construction is a separate, stronger-looking formulation. This question permits any deterministic simulator meeting the stated time and correctness requirements, without prescribing a generator or any other proof method.
